(Benefit)

[Heedlessness (al-dhuhul) and the difference between it and forgetfulness (al-nisyan)]

An example of heedlessness is a person who swears that he will not do something that is customary for him to do, but heedlessness and inattentiveness overcome him, so he does it.

The difference between this and the forgetful person is that the forgetful person has completely lost the oath from his mind, so he does what he swore against while remembering it and doing it deliberately; then he recalls that he had sworn to abstain from it. As for the heedless, the distracted and the diverted, they are not forgetful of their oath; rather, they have been diverted from it or have become oblivious, as a man becomes oblivious of something in his hand or lap through conversation, or by looking at something, or the like. As God the Exalted said: ﴿But as for one who came to you striving, and he fears [God], from him you are distracted﴾ [Abasa: 8–10].

It is said: lahā ʿan al-shayʾ yalhā, like ghashiya yaghshā, when he became inattentive to it; and lahā bihi yalhū, when he played with it. In the hadith, "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) became diverted by something that was in his hands," meaning he occupied himself with it. From the same root is the other hadith: "When God withholds something, He diverts [the one concerned] from it."

Al-Hasan was asked about the moisture that a man finds after ablution and istinja', and he said, "Be diverted from it."

Ibn al-Zubayr, whenever he heard the sound of thunder, would be diverted from his speech.

ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) said to a man whom he had sent with money to Abu ʿUbayda, and then said to the messenger: "Be diverted from him, then see what he does with it."

From the same usage is the verse of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

"Every friend I used to hope for said: 'I shall not distract you; indeed I am busy with you [i.e., occupied with my own concerns].'"

That is, I will not occupy you away from your affair and your matter.

In the Musnad:

"I asked my Lord that He not punish the lahhīn (those who are diverted) among my ummah."

And they are the bulha (simpletons), the heedless who did not deliberately commit sins.

It was also said: they are the children who have not committed any sin.

(Useful point)

Ahmad ibn Marwan al-Maliki reported from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about a deceased person who died without a shroud (kafan) being found for him, and he said: "He is to be placed face-down, and his face is not to be turned toward the qiblah."

I (Ibn al-Qayyim) say: This report is far from authentic from Abdullah ibn Abbas; rather it is baseless. The correct position is that he is covered with a barrier of earth, and he is placed in his grave (lahd) on his side, facing the qiblah, just as a naked person sleeps when a sheet or something else is spread over him. And when there is a barrier of earth over him while he faces the qiblah, he is in the position of one who is wearing his clothes.
God, glorified is He, made the human's contemplation of the bringing forth of his food from the earth a proof of His bringing him forth from it after his death, reasoning from like to like.
